studies.Population: Cancer-free UK Biobank men at recruitment
studies.Reference: Risk of cancer in regular and low meat-eaters, fish-eaters, and vegetarians: a prospective analysis of UK Biobank participants.
studies.Authors: Watling CZ, Schmidt JA, Dunneram Y, Tong TYN, Kelly RK, Knuppel A, Travis RC, Key TJ, Perez-Cornago A
studies.Timing: Diet assessed at recruitment; mean follow-up 11.4 years
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Participants were categorised into regular meat-eaters (n = 247,571), low meat-eaters (n = 205,385), fish-eaters (n = 10,696), and vegetarians (n = 8685) based on dietary questions completed at recruitment.

sample_size.excerpt: This left a total of 472,337 participants, of whom 217,937 were males and 254,400 were females.
sample_size.location: Methods, Study design and participants, Exclusions

cases.excerpt: After an average follow-up of 11.4 years, 54,961 incident cancers were identified, including 5882 colorectal, 7537 postmenopausal breast, and 9501 prostate cancers.

effect_size.excerpt: In men, being a fish-eater or a vegetarian was associated with a lower risk of prostate cancer (0.80, 0.65-0.99 and 0.69, 0.54-0.89, respectively).
